What is JEV?

A decision model

A general-purpose classifier from TypeSafe AI.
Fast, low-cost decisions for your application.

Context+Typed question→Structured decision
JEV is TypeSafe AI’s first System One model, introduced September 15, 2026. “General-purpose classifier” is a useful shorthand: it also supports rubric-based scoring and true/false probabilities. Sources: https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev and https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction

“Classifiers
have been around
forever!”

The skeptical interlude: classification is longstanding. The point is reducing the setup cost of putting a classifier into an application, not inventing classification. Image: The Simpsons, via https://laagenda.buenosaires.gob.ar/contenido/22021-gritarle-a-una-nube

Yes, that’s true

With JEV, you can define a new task
without collecting a training dataset.

Describe the decision

Provide context, a question, and the labels or rubric you care about.

Use a pretrained model

Start without fitting a separate classifier for each task.

Get probabilities directly

Typed outputs in parallel, rather than token-by-token text generation.

No task-specific training required to start. Evaluation on your own data still matters.

No training dataset means no task-specific dataset needed to configure the first call; it does not mean the underlying model was never trained. TypeSafe’s quickstart defines tasks using state and natural-language questions. Zero-shot setup is not unique to JEV. The distinction here combines that setup with a model built for structured probabilistic outputs. Type-safe does not mean always correct. Sources: https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/quickstart and https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev

Lowering the bar to use a classifier

Train your ownCollect labels · prepare data · fit a model
Start with JEVDescribe the decision · provide context · call the API

Less setup to get started. Evaluation still matters.

The high-jump metaphor refers to the barrier to entry, not lowering the standard of correctness. The comparison is with training a task-specific classifier. Other pretrained zero-shot classifiers and LLMs also reduce training-data requirements. TypeSafe confirms shared weights and request-based customization: https://docs.typesafe.ai/models . Illustration generated for this presentation.

Regression predicts a number

Learn a relationship
from examples.

Each dot is an observation.
The fitted line estimates a score for a given number of study hours.

Synthetic teaching data · least-squares fit

The line is fitted to 15 synthetic observations by ordinary least squares, minimizing squared vertical errors. This is linear regression, not autoregression. A relationship in the data does not establish causation.

Autoregression uses what came before

Predict the next value from earlier values
in the same sequence.

Yesterday→Today→Tomorrow?

In time series

Past measurements help forecast the next measurement.

In language models

Earlier tokens provide context for predicting the next token.

In JEV

Outputs are structured decisions, produced in parallel.

Classical autoregressive models regress a time series on its own lagged values. Autoregressive language generation similarly conditions each next token on preceding tokens, but is not simply a straight-line time-series model. Sources: https://otexts.com/fpp3/AR.html and https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev

A classifier predicts a category

Regression

What number?

An estimated fare: £32

Classification

Which category?

Survived or did not survive

A classifier can estimate class probabilities.
A decision rule turns those probabilities into a label.

Examples are illustrative, not model outputs. Classification predicts discrete labels; regression predicts a numeric target. Logistic regression, despite its name, is commonly used for classification. Source: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/compose/plot_column_transformer_mixed_types.html

1. Prepare the data & hold some back

Separate the examples used to learn from the examples used to test.

Training data · 80%Test data · 20%

Choose features

Start with age, recorded sex, and ticket class.

Prepare inputs

Fill missing ages and encode categories using training data only.

Protect the test set

Keep its outcomes hidden until the model is ready to evaluate.

An 80/20 split is an illustrative choice, not a result computed for this presentation. Stratify the random split by survival to preserve class proportions. Fit preprocessing on training data only, then apply the same transformation to the test set. For model selection, use cross-validation inside the training set and reserve the test set for final evaluation. Source: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split.html

2. Train a classifier

For example, use logistic regression.
It learns how to combine features into a probability.

Passenger
features→Learned
weights→Probability
of survival

Predict

Make predictions on the training examples.

Measure error

Compare probabilities with known survival labels.

Adjust

Update weights to reduce the training loss.

This is a conceptual training walkthrough; no model has been fitted to the Titanic data in this deck. Logistic regression applies a sigmoid to a weighted sum of features and optimizes a classification loss, typically with regularization. Despite its name, it is a classifier here. Source: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/compose/plot_column_transformer_mixed_types.html

3. Test on passengers it has not seen

Run the held-out features through the trained model.
Then compare predictions with the hidden labels.

Choose a decision rule

For illustration: predict survival when its probability is at least 0.5.

Count the errors

Inspect correct predictions, false positives, and false negatives.

Compare with a baseline

Does it beat always predicting the most common class?

Good training performance alone does not show that a model generalizes.

Threshold 0.5 is illustrative, not universally optimal. Choose thresholds using training/validation data based on the costs of different errors. Report held-out metrics and inspect probability calibration if probabilities will drive decisions. No accuracy result is claimed here. Source: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/compose/plot_column_transformer_mixed_types.html

Back to JEV: describe the task

Task-specific classifier

Collect labeled examples
Prepare features
Fit a model
Evaluate

Pretrained decision model

Provide context
Describe labels or a rubric
Call JEV
Evaluate

You can skip task-specific training.
You still need to test the decisions.

JEV is already trained. Its quickstart configures a new task through state, questions, and criteria rather than training a task-specific classifier. This is not a claim that JEV beats a trained classifier on Titanic. Zero-shot classification is also possible with other pretrained models. Sources: https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/quickstart and https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction

The JEV API contract

POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone

You send

model Which JEV version

state Passenger features

questions The decision and allowed labels

→

You receive

choice One of your labels

probabilities A value for each label

confidence How concentrated the distribution is

Context in. A decision and probabilities out.

Choice request and response contract: https://docs.typesafe.ai/api . Confidence is distinct from the probability of the selected class; it summarizes concentration of the distribution and is not a guarantee of correctness. See https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence . In this experiment, a local Python process acted as the client; the browser does not call the API.

So, how did it do?

One fixed prompt. No labeled examples supplied. No task-specific training.

Accuracy on the same 100 rows · jev-1.13.0 · median API call: 371 ms

JEV beat the majority baseline, but not the simple sex-based rule.

Actual run, completed 2026-09-24T01:59:08.950414+00:00. Kaggle Titanic train.csv from a public mirror, 891 labeled rows. Seed 20260923; stratified sample of 62 non-survivors and 38 survivors. Seven features: Pclass, Sex, Age, SibSp, Parch, Fare, Embarked; no Name, PassengerId, Ticket, Cabin, or Survived sent. No tuning or retries. All 100 requests succeeded. Accuracy uses API choice. Majority baseline 62/100; female-survives heuristic 74/100; JEV 72/100. No trained logistic-regression comparator was run. Approximate Wilson 95% interval for JEV accuracy: 62.5–79.9%; this is descriptive and does not address pretraining contamination. Request latency includes client/network overhead, using two concurrent requests. Input tokens 49,260; output tokens 4,070. Dataset: https://github.com/dsindy/kaggle-titanic/blob/master/data/train.csv . Competition: https://www.kaggle.com/c/titanic/data

Confusion matrix computed from all 100 persisted API responses and labels joined only after inference. Survival recall 20/38 = 52.6%. Non-survival recall 52/62 = 83.9%. Brier score 0.231535 for P(survived); no calibration claim is made. This is not a Kaggle leaderboard submission, and the unlabeled Kaggle test.csv was not used. Full predictions and raw requests/responses are saved alongside the presentation.

Small decisions, fast

An alternative to LLM calls for classification, scoring, and routing.

in our Titanic experiment
≈ $0.0021Estimated API cost
for all 100 predictions

Use JEV for bounded decisions.
Keep an LLM for writing and extended reasoning.

Cost calculated from token usage and published pricing. No LLM speed comparison was run.

Measured median client-observed API request latency: 370.5 ms; p95: 418 ms; two concurrent requests. Cost estimate: 49,260 input tokens × $0.042 / 1,000,000 = $0.00206892, about 0.207 cents for 100 calls. Output tokens free under published pricing; this is a list-price estimate, not a verified invoice. Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/models . TypeSafe positions JEV for fast structured decisions: https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev . We did not measure a relative speedup, price ratio, or accuracy comparison against an LLM.

Recent transcript
Text + rubric
→
JEV
Score each dimension
→
Application
Update the scorecard

Clear explanation?

Score whether the speaker explains the idea clearly.

Evidence provided?

Score whether claims are supported in the transcript.

Question answered?

Check whether the response addresses the question.

Your code combines scores and handles uncertain answers.

Illustrative transcript application, not an implemented integration or measured streaming benchmark. TypeSafe documents real-time applications and transcript analysis: https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/use-case-map . Composite scoring evaluates independent dimensions and combines scores with application-owned weights: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring . JEV takes text, so live audio must first be transcribed. Debounce transcript updates and evaluate a bounded recent context. Latency depends on input size and workload.

Speculative fan-out for data queries

Ask about possible query branches together.
Use only the answers relevant to the chosen branch.

“Show revenue in Europe last quarter”
Which metric?
RevenueWhich region?
EuropeWhich time window?
Last quarterIf orders: which status?
Ignored
One JEV call → code selects an approved query template → database

Questions run independently against the same context; code selects the applicable results.

Adapted example, not a measured database integration. Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out . Ask intent and branch-specific questions in one call instead of sequential round trips. Every question must be answerable from the original state; it cannot depend on another question’s answer in the same call. Supply finite metric/region/date-window options, convert dates in code, and use parameterized query templates and normal permissions. Fan-out here speculates on model questions; it does not run every database query or generate arbitrary SQL. TypeSafe says extra questions usually have little latency impact, not zero resource cost.

Decision gating

A prediction proposes an action.
Application rules decide whether to proceed.

JEV decision
Label + uncertainty
→
Policy in code
Risk + tested threshold
→
Act or escalate
Proceed · clarify · review

Clear, low-risk match

Apply a support-ticket label automatically.

Ambiguous request

Ask a clarifying question or use a stronger model.

Consequential action

Require the normal authorization and review checks.

Choose thresholds using your own evaluation data; confidence is not a permission check.

Adapted from TypeSafe confidence-gated routing: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/confidence-routing . Confidence describes distribution concentration and should be interpreted in the context of the task: https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence . No universal threshold guarantees safety or accuracy. Combine label, probabilities, confidence and action-specific policy; retain deterministic authorization.

Smart routing for an agent

Classify intent and complexity before invoking expensive tools.

“Where is my order?”→Database lookup
“Compare these products”→Specialist LLM
Unclear or complex request→Stronger model or human

No training dataset to get started.
You still need evals on your own use case.

Try it on one small decision. Measure accuracy, latency, and cost before relying on it.

Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/intent-routing . TypeSafe describes intent and complexity classification followed by deterministic code, specialist LLMs, or human escalation. These are illustrative routes; validate routing quality and end-to-end latency/cost for the actual workload. The closing thesis: JEV lowers task-specific data/training overhead and offers a fast, low-cost decision option for some work otherwise sent to LLMs.
